ch10.anchor: a cold wind and a bitter rain
ch10.note: The chapter opens on a four-part play on the Chinese figures that pair wind with rain. Chen Duxiu’s years were hufeng-huanyu, “summoning wind and rain,” commanding events at will; Qu Qiubai’s brief tenure a “violent storm”; Xiang Zhongfa’s a “foul wind and bloody rain,” a reign of terror; and Bo Gu’s a qifeng-kuyu, a “cold wind and bitter rain,” the set phrase for wretched, comfortless times.

Ruijin, a town in southern Jiangxi, was the seat of the Central Revolutionary Base, or Central Soviet — the largest of the Communist rural bases and, from November 1931, capital of the self-proclaimed Chinese Soviet Republic. It was the destination of the underground courier lines this chapter describes, and the starting point, in 1934, of the Long March.

Zhang Wentian (1900–1976), who wrote under the name Luo Fu, one of the Moscow-trained “Twenty-eight Bolsheviks.” He took over as the Party’s general secretary in early 1935, after the Zunyi conference, and later served as a diplomat and vice foreign minister.
Qin Guan (1049–1100), styled Shaoyou, a major lyric (ci) poet of the Northern Song and one of the disciples gathered around Su Shi. The line of descent is the Qin family’s own claim.

Qin Jin (1467–1544), styled Fengshan, a high official under the Ming Jiajing emperor. The family phrase renders his career: he headed five of the boards across the Ming’s two capitals, Beijing and Nanjing (each kept a parallel set of Six Boards), and rose to the honorary rank of Grand Guardian (taibao). The Jichang Garden his family laid out survives in Wuxi as one of the country’s celebrated classical gardens.
Qin Jiacong (English name Frank Ching), a journalist and a descendant of the same Wuxi Qin line, whose family history traces the clan across some nine centuries.

An echo of the May Fourth attack on Confucian ritualism — the “rites that eat people” of Lu Xun’s Diary of a Madman (1918). Bo Gu, writing here as “Shanglin” in 1925, was a student caught up in that iconoclasm.

ch10.anchor: bleak and forlorn and steeped in grief
ch10.note: The phrase is Li Qingzhao’s, the opening reduplicatives of her famous song lyric “Note After Note” (Sheng sheng man) — a byword in Chinese for desolate grief.

“Changlin” is Bo Gu, whom his mother knew by his childhood name; the memoirist Qin Moya is his eldest daughter. Bo Gu died on April 8, 1946, in the air crash at Heicha Mountain in Xingxian, Shanxi, that killed a group of Party leaders returning from the Chongqing talks — the “April 8 martyrs.” His mother, kept in the dark, went on waiting for him.

Huarun, in English China Resources, grew out of the Party’s underground trading network described in this chapter; today it is a state-owned conglomerate among the Fortune Global 500. Qin Bangli (1908–1968), Bo Gu’s younger brother, ran it under the alias Yang Lin; the chapter follows him from a Wuxi money house to the founding of the firm.

The Sino-French Drugstore (Zhongfa Yaofang) was a well-known Western-style pharmacy chain in Republican Shanghai; a branch in the treaty port of Shantou, in eastern Guangdong, gave the Party a respectable commercial front and a waystation on the sea route south.

ch10.anchor: escorted several hundred comrades in all through enemy-held territory
ch10.note: The names that follow are a roll-call of the men who would run the People’s Republic — among them Zhou Enlai, Deng Xiaoping, Liu Shaoqi, and Hu Yaobang, and the future marshals Ye Jianying, Liu Bocheng, and Nie Rongzhen — passed one by one along this single courier line into the Jiangxi base.

ch10.anchor: took the train on to Shaoyang
ch10.note: Shaoyang is in central Hunan, far off this Guangdong-to-Fujian route; the name as printed in the Biography of Chen Yun is almost certainly a slip, most likely for a place near Shantou. —Trans.

ch10.anchor: chief of the executive section of the Central Political Security Bureau
ch10.note: The Central Political Security Bureau, formed in 1931, was the security and counter-intelligence organ of the Jiangxi Soviet — a separate body from the Shanghai Special Branch, and a forerunner of the Party’s later state-security apparatus. It ran its own courier lines, which is the crux of the author’s argument here: the “Chen Pannian” of these accounts belongs to it and is not the famous Pan Hannian.

ch10.anchor: good at building a new one
ch10.note: Both slogans are Mao Zedong’s, from 1949. The first paraphrases “Farewell, Leighton Stuart” (August 1949), whose received text reads “Blockade us for eight or ten years and all of China’s problems will be solved”; the book gives “decades.” The second is from his opening address to the Chinese People’s Political Consultative Conference in September 1949, on the eve of the People’s Republic.
